title: Functions and Responsibilities of the Nurse in the Primary Health Care Setting
path: Functions and Responsibilities of the Nurse in the Primary Health Care Setting

headings.title: Introduction to Primary Health Care and the Nurse's Role
headings.content:
Primary Health Care represents the first level of contact individuals, families, and communities have with the national health system, bringing health care as close as possible to where people live and work. In Nigeria, the PHC system forms the bedrock of the national health policy, designed to deliver comprehensive, accessible, and culturally acceptable services. Within this decentralized structure, the nurse often functions as the administrative head, clinical care provider, and community liaison rolled into one.

Unlike hospital-based nursing that typically deals with acute, specialized pathology, PHC nursing centers on wellness promotion, early disease detection, and continuous community engagement. The nurse assesses local health indices, identifies vulnerable populations, and coordinates care with village health workers and traditional birth attendants. Success in this setting depends heavily on understanding social determinants of health, such as local agricultural cycles, clean water availability, and prevailing socioeconomic conditions.

headings.title: Core Principles of PHC Guiding Nursing Practice
headings.content:
- **Equitable distribution**: Essential health services must be shared equally among all segments of the population, regardless of wealth or location.
- **Community participation**: The local population must be actively involved in planning, implementing, and evaluating their own health programs.
- **Health promotion**: Actions focus on addressing root causes of illness rather than merely treating established pathology.
- **Appropriate technology**: Methods, equipment, and care delivery must be scientifically sound, adaptable, and affordable for the local community.
- **Intersectoral collaboration**: Health cannot be achieved in isolation; cooperation with agriculture, education, and sanitation sectors is mandatory.

headings.title: Clinical and Curative Nursing Duties in the PHC Clinic
headings.content:
The PHC clinic manages a high volume of everyday ailments, requiring the nurse to master syndromic management and nurse-initiated treatment protocols. Common presentations include uncomplicated malaria, acute respiratory infections, diarrheal diseases, and minor skin infections. The nurse performs thorough physical assessments, dispenses standing-order medications, and recognizes danger signs that warrant immediate referral to secondary general hospitals.

Beyond acute episodic care, clinic nurses manage chronic stable conditions such as mild hypertension and uncomplicated type 2 diabetes through regular monitoring and lifestyle counseling. Effective triage prevents clinic congestion and ensures that severe emergencies receive rapid stabilization before transport. Documentation must remain concise yet comprehensive to maintain continuity of care across varying shift rotations.

headings.title: Maternal, Newborn, and Child Health Services
headings.content:
Safeguarding the health of mothers and children forms a massive pillar of daily workload in Nigerian primary health centers. Antenatal care (ANC) visits provide opportunities for routine screening, iron and folate supplementation, intermittent preventive treatment for malaria in pregnancy (IPTp), and tetanus toxoid immunization. Nurses educate expectant mothers on birth preparedness, complication readiness, and the importance of skilled birth attendance.

Postnatal care focuses on monitoring uterine involution, establishing breastfeeding, and assessing neonatal vitality. Under-five clinics provide growth monitoring charts (often called road-to-health cards) to track nutritional status, detect failure to thrive early, and manage childhood illnesses using integrated management of childhood illnesses (IMCI) guidelines.

headings.title: Disease Surveillance, Immunization, and Preventive Care
headings.content:
Surveillance acts as an early warning radar for public health emergencies. The PHC nurse is responsible for identifying and immediately reporting priority diseases such as measles, cholera, yellow fever, and acute flaccid paralysis to local government health authorities. Prompt reporting prevents localized outbreaks from escalating into regional epidemics.

Routine immunization under the Expanded Programme on Immunization (EPI) protects infants and women of childbearing age against vaccine-preventable diseases. Cold chain maintenance is an operational priority; a compromised vaccine refrigerator ruins potent biologicals, wasting scarce resources and leaving communities vulnerable. Nurses also spearhead environmental health campaigns, inspecting local water sources and promoting proper waste disposal.

headings.title: Community Mobilization, Health Education, and Advocacy
headings.content:
Sustainable health improvements require active community buy-in rather than top-down imposition. The nurse engages community leaders, religious groups, and youth organizations to discuss prevailing health challenges, such as reluctance toward vaccination or poor sanitation practices. Health education sessions are tailored to local languages and cultural idioms, utilizing storytelling, drama, and visual aids rather than dense medical jargon.

Advocacy involves championing the health needs of marginalized populations to local government councils and traditional rulers. By securing resources for borehole repairs, clearing blocked drainage systems, or supporting insecticide-treated net distribution, the nurse addresses the fundamental social roots of disease.

headings.title: Leadership, Management, and Interprofessional Collaboration
headings.content:
Running a primary health center requires multifaceted administrative competence. The nurse manager oversees facility inventory, tracks drug stock levels to prevent expiration or stock-outs, manages staff rosters, and maintains accurate health management information system (HMIS) records. Data collected at the facility level feeds into district and national health databases, guiding policy formulation and resource allocation.

Collaboration with community health extension workers (CHEWs), environmental health officers, and laboratory technicians is vital for seamless operations. The nurse provides mentorship, delegates appropriate tasks, and resolves interpersonal conflicts to maintain a functional, harmonious team environment.

headings.title: Challenges and Ethical Considerations for the PHC Nurse
headings.content:
Practicing in primary health care settings exposes nurses to unique systemic hurdles and ethical dilemmas. Common operational challenges include erratic electricity supply, poor road infrastructure hindering outreach, delayed salary disbursements, and chronic shortages of essential medicines. Despite these obstacles, nurses must uphold professional ethics, maintaining patient confidentiality in tight-knit rural communities where gossip travels fast.

Cultural beliefs often clash with orthodox medical advice, requiring the nurse to navigate sensitive situations with patience and respect rather than outright condemnation. Balancing limited resources while advocating for the most vulnerable patients demands resilience, moral courage, and dedication to the ideals of public health.
